headline: Stock Slide Nudges Rates Lower as Fed Hike Talk Grows
tileReason: The daily 30-year average dipped to 7.48% Tuesday as a stock sell-off sent money into bonds; this morning Fed Governor Waller floated a bigger December hike, keeping the 10-year yield near 5.10%.
takeaway:
Rates eased a little Tuesday. The daily 30-year average slipped to 7.48% Tuesday from 7.51% Monday, a small dip that keeps rates close to their highest in over a month. Other trackers sit lower: Mortgage Research Center shows about 7.36% this morning and Zillow showed 7.40% Tuesday afternoon.

A stock sell-off helped bonds on Tuesday. Stocks fell sharply, with the Dow down about 1.6%, after a brief outage at a classified National Security Agency network rattled investors ahead of Nvidia's earnings (the agency later blamed scheduled maintenance). Some money moved into the safety of bonds, and the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed near 5.10% Tuesday, down from about 5.12% Monday.

Lenders passed along only a sliver of that. The bond rally was modest and came mid-day, and lenders tend to reprice only when bonds move a lot during the day. Weekly data out this morning from the Mortgage Bankers Association show its average 30-year contract rate jumped to 7.35% last week from 7.21%, and applications fell 2.3%.

This morning brought a new push toward higher rates. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview today that inflation is spreading into services and the Fed should consider a half-point hike in December, or clearly signal more increases in January and beyond. October housing starts also came in stronger than expected at a 1.31 million yearly pace, though single-family permits, a sign of future building, fell. The 10-year yield is about 5.09% to 5.12% this morning, close to Tuesday's level.

A December hike is all but certain. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point hike in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 96% to 97% this morning, with the rest on a bigger half-point move. New York Fed President John Williams has pushed back on a half-point move, so officials don't all agree on the pace.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.10% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 13, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff.

The next tests come quickly. The Treasury sells $16 billion of 20-year bonds at 10 AM PT today, and minutes of the Fed's October meeting come out at 11 AM PT; both could move rates this afternoon. After that: Freddie Mac's weekly survey Thursday, the Fed's preferred inflation measure on Nov 25, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via ChainCatcher (Nov 18, 06:23); CME FedWatch via 24/7 Wall St. (Nov 17 close and Nov 18); Trading Economics (Nov 18)
fedOdds.note: These are the odds of a quarter-point hike. CME FedWatch showed 96.8% early Wednesday, with 3.2% on a half-point move, so a hike of some size is close to 100%. 24/7 Wall St. cited about 95% at Tuesday's close and 96% Wednesday; Trading Economics shows about 96%. One newsletter cited 92% on Tuesday morning, so readings differ by source. Fed Governor Waller's call for a possible half-point hike came after some of these readings.

drivers.title: Fed officials keep calling for more hikes
drivers.text: Fed Governor Waller said today the Fed should consider a half-point hike in December or clearly signal more increases, and St. Louis Fed President Musalem says several more are likely by spring. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row, and wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Economy still showing strength
drivers.text: Housing starts jumped to a 1.31 million yearly pace in October, beating forecasts, and shoppers kept spending outside car dealers. A sturdy economy gives the Fed less reason to ease up, which keeps upward pressure on yields.

drivers.title: Stock sell-off sent money into bonds
drivers.text: Stocks fell for a fourth straight day Tuesday, hit by a brief NSA network outage and worries about AI companies. When investors sell stocks, some of that money goes into Treasury bonds, pushing yields and mortgage rates down a bit.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.10% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 13, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 17 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, with a slight lean higher. Mortgage rates dipped to about 7.48% Tuesday, and the 10-year Treasury yield is holding near 5.10%. Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is close to fully expected, Governor Waller is now raising the idea of a bigger half-point move, inflation reports keep running hot and housing starts beat forecasts. In borrowers' favor: stocks have fallen four days in a row, which tends to push money into bonds, and mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.10% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Big swing events: today's Fed minutes and 20-year bond sale, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average dipped to 7.48% Tuesday, still near its highest in over a month but below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Fed officials are now debating how big December's rate increase should be, so the next few weeks could be bumpy. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are holding near 7.5%, and mortgage applications fell last week as rates climbed, so buyers are feeling the pinch. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out heading into the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates dipped slightly to about 7.48% as stocks slid, but Fed talk of a bigger December rate hike keeps the pressure on.
